subject: digital-logic
subtopics: fixed-point addition and subtraction in hardware, and the signed overflow test (carry into the sign column against carry out of it)
unsigned shift-and-add multiplication, the 2n-bit product, and the array multiplier's delay
Booth recoding: the pair table, the run-of-ones identity, and the step-by-step algorithm
the count of additions and subtractions Booth's algorithm performs, and the worst and best multiplier patterns
restoring division and the restore step
non-restoring division, its quotient-digit set and its final correction
fixed-point fractional (Q-format) multiplication and the shift back to the input format
floating-point addition and subtraction: alignment, normalisation, rounding
floating-point multiplication and division: significands, biased exponents, sign
IEEE rounding modes, guard, round and sticky bits, and the ulp
precision loss: absorption, catastrophic cancellation and non-associativity
fixed point against floating point: range, spacing and relative error

chosen.title: GATE CSE Book, Digital Logic chapter - computer arithmetic, real-number representation and Booth algorithm
chosen.channel: GATE Overflow (Arjun Suresh, Praneeth, Ananya Mukhopadhyay and the GATE CSE members)
covers: carry against overflow, and the condition Cout XOR Cn-1 = 1 with its same-sign restatement
the IEEE 754 single-precision layout, the bias and the implied leading 1, worked on 0.75
the Booth pair table, the run-of-ones identity 2^(k+1) - 2^m, and the full 01011 x 01110 trace reaching 154
radix-4 Booth recoding with the three-bit table, and the b/2 additions and b/2 subtractions worst case
the note that the alternating pattern is the worst case for Booth
the ROM size for a multiplier table, which is carded under Combinational Circuits
chosen.why: The only source read this run that states the GATE-level facts in GATE's own words and then works a full Booth trace. Its overflow condition, its Booth trace and its worst-case sentence are the three claims that the overflow and Booth cards are built on, and its radix-4 table is the material behind the operation-count card's last remember line. Read in part: the whole of sections 2.2.7 to 2.2.10, which is the digital-logic half of the book, and nothing beyond.

chosen.title: Lecture 39 - Floating-Point Arithmetic
chosen.channel: NPTEL, Computer Architecture and Organization (Prof. Indranil Sengupta, IIT Kharagpur)
covers: floating-point addition and subtraction as one procedure: compare the exponents, shift the smaller mantissa right by the difference, add or subtract, normalise
the 270.75 + 2.375 worked example and the 224 - 270.75 example that needs a three-place left shift after the subtraction
the adder's hardware: an 8-bit exponent ALU, a comparator, a right shifter, an add/subtract unit and a normaliser
multiplication: add the two exponents and subtract the bias once, multiply the mantissas, XOR the signs, normalise
division: subtract the exponents, add the bias once, divide the mantissas, normalise
the 24-bit multiplier and divider, and the four rounding modes (truncation, ceiling, floor, round) with the MIPS instructions that select them
chosen.why: The only lecture transcript of this topic whose text could be read at all this run, and it is the sequence the syllabus line describes: addition, then multiplication, then division, then rounding. It supplies the two worked addition examples that make the alignment step concrete and the double-bias correction that the multiplication card turns on. Read in part: the served text runs from the opening through the addition hardware and the first half of the rounding discussion, then jumps to the MIPS material, so the middle of the lecture is missing and nothing is claimed about it.

chosen.title: Chapter 8: Computer Arithmetic (Part II) - integer division, floating-point addition, multiplication, division and rounding
chosen.channel: Prof. Smruti Ranjan Sarangi, IIT Delhi, Basic Computer Architecture (slides read through a published slide transcript)
covers: the division properties R < D and Q maximal, and the reduction N = DQ + R
the restoring algorithm with the 00111 / 0011 trace reaching quotient 0010 and remainder 0001, and its proof
the non-restoring algorithm, its 11101 ... 11110 trace on the same division, the divergence proof, and the closing U = U + D correction
the 25-bit working register for addition, alignment by shifting the smaller significand, and renormalisation after a carry
the four IEEE rounding modes with the increment condition for each, guard, round and sticky bits, and renormalisation after rounding
the 2.34 x 10^2 + 0.0256 x 10^2 rounding example that differs with and without guard bits
floating-point multiplication as E1 + E2 - bias and division as E1 - E2 + bias, with the sign as the XOR
the 0.5 x -0.75 multiplication example, and the normal and denormal forms 1 <= P < 2 and 0 <= P < 1
chosen.why: The only source read this run that teaches both division algorithms with a complete worked trace and a proof, and the only one that gives the guard, round and sticky increment rule. Four cards rest on it: the two division cards, the rounding card and the multiplication card. Read in part: the transcript carries the division section, the addition and rounding sections and the multiplication section; the floating-point division and Goldschmidt material at the end was not needed and is not claimed.

chosen.title: Unit 7 Computer Arithmetic - addition and subtraction, Booth multiplication, division, floating-point operations
chosen.channel: Prof. Chirag Bhalodia, CO 2140707, following Mano's Digital Design
covers: fixed point and floating point as the two data types, and the point as an interpretation of the same bits
signed-magnitude addition and subtraction with the E and AVF flip-flops, and the statement that integer arithmetic is done in signed two's complement
Booth's rules in Mano's wording: subtract on the first 1 of a run, add on the first 0, and the 001110 = 2^4 - 2^1 identity
the restoring division steps: shift, subtract, test the sign, restore or set the bit
the rules of floating-point multiplication (add the exponents and subtract the bias) and division (subtract the exponents), and the note that no overflow check is needed
chosen.why: The only source read this run that gives Mano's register-level framing - the E and AVF flip-flops, the signed-magnitude path, and the explicit statement that machines do integer arithmetic in two's complement while floating-point mantissas are sign-magnitude. That framing is what the overflow card's first two remember lines rest on, and its Booth rules confirm the GATE Overflow pair table from a second, independent text. Read in part: the outline, the addition and subtraction section, the Booth section, the division steps and the floating-point multiplication and division rules; the BCD adder and decimal arithmetic unit at the end are outside this topic.

chosen.title: What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic
chosen.channel: David Goldberg, ACM Computing Surveys 23(1), March 1991
covers: why a real number is not representable: the infinite binary expansion of 0.1, and the out-of-range case
normalised form, the significand against the older word mantissa, and the need to reserve one exponent value for zero
relative error measured in ulps against machine epsilon, and the wobble of the ulp error by a factor of the base
guard digits, and Theorem 1 that a subtraction without a guard digit has relative error as large as the base minus one
Theorem 2: one guard digit bounds the relative error of a sum or difference by 2 epsilon
benign against catastrophic cancellation, and the requirement that basic operations be correctly rounded
chosen.why: The only source read this run that explains why the ulp is the right measure and why cancellation is catastrophic rather than merely inaccurate, and the one that states the two theorems the rounding card's error bound rests on. The precision-loss card and the fixed-versus-floating card both draw on it. Read in part: sections 1.1 to 1.5, the rounding-error chapter, and the opening of the IEEE standard chapter; the systems-aspects and details chapters were not read.

chosen.title: Booth Algorithm kya hai? - Computer Architecture (Booth algorithm in Hindi)
covers: Booth as a multiplication algorithm for two signed integers held in two's complement
the run-of-ones identity, a string of 1s from weight 2^k to 2^m read as 2^(k+1) - 2^m
the register set: multiplicand in M, multiplier in Q, AC cleared, one extra bit q(-1) cleared, and a sequence counter SC
the three pair cases: 00 or 11 shift only, 01 adds the multiplicand to AC, 10 subtracts it
the result appearing in the AC and QR registers
chosen.why: Chosen deliberately so the topic is not built from English alone, and it is the only non-English source read this run. It is the clearest short statement in any of the six sources of the register set and of the three pair cases, which is the vocabulary a large part of the GATE audience meets first. Read in full and translated into English here; every claim it contributes is recomputed in scripts/validate.py, because a translation sits between the source and the reader. Two statements in it are wrong against the standard treatment - that q(-1) is 'Qn incremented by 1', and that the loop stops after 'n-1 bits' - so neither is used, and the disagreement is recorded on the card rather than smoothed over.

M. Morris Mano, Computer System Architecture - Booth's algorithm and the division algorithms, the source of the q(-1) register and the arithmetic-shift wording

David A. Patterson and John L. Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, chapter 3 - the floating-point addition flowchart (compare exponents, shift, add, normalise, round, check for overflow) that the addition card follows
David Goldberg, 'What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic', ACM Computing Surveys 23(1), 1991
IEEE 754-2019, the standard for the rounding modes and the required correct rounding of the five basic operations
GATE 2027 CS syllabus, Digital Logic line 'number representation and arithmetic (fixed and floating point)'
Official GATE CSE papers and answer keys for the twelve recorded questions - not fetched this run, which is why every PYQ here is SOURCED rather than key-verified
notes: The syllabus names this topic in nine words, 'number representation and arithmetic (fixed and floating point)', so the twelve subtopics above are this run's enumeration from the standard treatment (Mano's arithmetic chapters, the IIT Delhi chapter 8 outline) and from the GATE question record - not a quotation from the syllabus. The representation half of the line was carded by an earlier run in Number Systems and is not repeated here; every card in this topic is about an operation.

Twelve GATE CSE previous-year questions were verified, from 1996 to 2026, and every one is SOURCED against an accepted answer rather than key-verified against an official paper, so no marks field comes from an official key and question references follow the paper numbering where two independent paper listings agree, with the GATE Overflow number recorded where it differs.

No video transcript was readable this run, so videoRefs is empty on all twelve cards and the six chosen sources are lecture transcripts, published slide decks and texts that were read as text. Three of the six are Indian university material (NPTEL IIT Kharagpur, IIT Delhi) and one is a Hindi article.

One non-English source was readable and it was read in full: the eHindiStudy article on Booth's algorithm in Hindi, translated here and marked as translated on the card it feeds. It supplies the register set and the three pair cases only; every number it touches is recomputed in scripts/validate.py.

Five cards carry no previous-year question because no verified CSE question is decided by them alone: the Booth recoding card (the two Booth questions test the count, and they sit on the next card), restoring division, non-restoring division, the Q-format card and the rounding card. Each says so in its source line rather than borrowing a question that does not test it.

The visual lesson animates floating-point addition on the exact operands of GATE CSE 2026 Set 1 Q.26, so the animation and a verified PYQ share one computation. Its exponent fields, the two-place alignment shift, the significand sum, the resulting word and the absorption case are all recomputed in scripts/validate.py.

One source statement is recorded rather than adopted: the Mano-based deck says floating-point multiplication needs no overflow check. That is true of the significand, which cannot exceed 4, and false of the exponent, which does overflow. The multiplication card states the narrower claim and says why.
